claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 wt% yttrium and applying an oxidizing anneal at approximately 800°C for 1 hour in air will form Y2O3 precipitates in WNbMoTaTi.
The in-situ-formed Y2O3 precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly dispersed.
Y2O3 precipitates will form both within grains and along grain boundaries.
Y2O3 particles act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
The Y2O3 particles capture radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Capturing vacancies and interstitials mitigates the formation of radiation-induced defect clusters.
The proposed defect-sink mechanism reduces radiation-induced void swelling.
The proposed defect-sink mechanism reduces irradiation-induced hardening.
A nanoscale, uniform Y2O3 distribution helps preserve the alloy's ductility and strength.
Under irradiation at approximately 500°C up to 1 dpa, the modified alloy will exhibit at least 30% less void swelling than the unmodified baseline.
Under irradiation at approximately 500°C up to 1 dpa, the modified alloy will exhibit at least 30% less irradiation-induced hardening than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will retain tensile strength comparable to that of the original alloy.
The modified alloy will retain ductility comparable to that of the original alloy.
The proposed improvement depends on ball milling, HIP near 1200°C, and the controlled oxidizing anneal.
Irradiation at approximately 500°C up to 1 dpa mimics plasma-facing conditions in fusion reactors.
Variability in the oxidizing heat treatment may cause Y2O3 particle coarsening or an uneven particle distribution.
Y2O3 particle coarsening or uneven distribution could compromise the predicted radiation-tolerance improvement.
